Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have expanded its role in scientific research, enabling systems to analyze data, identify patterns, and even propose hypotheses. 1 Yet, most of these models operate within fixed objectives and have limited ability to deliberate about scientific questions or adapt their strategies based on outcomes. Reasoning, the process of evaluating competing hypotheses and designing informative experiments, is central to genuine scientific exploration.

citations.snippet: By training neural networks with billions or trillions of parameters, studies have found that LLMs have demonstrated long text generation capabilities that far exceed traditional language modeling tasks [17][18][19][20][21] and have gradually expanded to more complex task areas, as shown in Figure 1b. Specifically, LLM usually has four core capabilities: (1) cognitive capabilities, which can efficiently understand and process long contexts [26,27]; (2) cross-language capabilities, which can generalize across languages, translate text, and achieve knowledge transfer between different languages [28]; (3) multitask capabilities, which can be applied to multiple language understanding and generation tasks such as text classification, information extraction, and question-answering reasoning [29][30][31][32]; and (4) generation capabilities, which can generate high-quality, logically coherent, and creative text content [33,34]. Benefiting from these capabilities, LLMs applications have expanded far beyond simple text generation and dialogue systems.

LLMs built on transformer architectures demonstrate general intelligence capabilities by leveraging massive datasets, large-scale neural networks, self-supervised learning, and powerful hardware [17]. Representative proprietary models include GPT-4 by OpenAI [18], Gemini by Google [19], and Claude 3 by Anthropic [20]; while open-source models include LLaMA 2 by Meta [21] and DeepSeek-V3 by DeepSeek [22]. These models leverage extensive knowledge acquired during pretraining and are capable of processing diverse data types, including text, images, and molecular structures.

Scientific discovery has long relied on human expertise, with foundational equations such as the Hall-Petch equation [1] in metallurgy and the Arrhenius equation [2] in chemical kinetics emerging from close attention to experimental data. In 1889, Arrhenius examined published temperaturedependent reaction-rate data and showed that several datasets could be described by a common relation.

For decades, researchers have hoped that artificial intelligence (AI) could help speed up the full scientific workflow, from data generation and hypothesis building to equation discovery and experimental validation. Early practical progress came through machine learning, which benefited from the rapid growth of materials data through high-throughput experiments [3], databases such as the Materials Project [4], and broader efforts such as the Materials Genome Initiative [5]. These tools have been applied to many problems, including prediction of metal fatigue properties [6] and thermodynamic stability of inorganic compounds [7].

fulltextExcerpts: Large language models (LLMs) introduce a different kind of capability for materials science. Because they are trained on large collections of web text, scientific papers, textbooks, and technical documents, they can draw from a wide range of scientific knowledge rather than from a single taskspecific dataset. In materials science, LLM-based agents have so far been used mainly for extracting information from the literature [12,13,14,15,16,17,18].

By evaluating OpenAI's Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) models on materials science datasets of different complexity, this work provides a quantitative picture of the current strengths and limits of LLM-based scientific knowledge as a basis for autonomous scientific workflows.

Using this framework, we study several materials science datasets governed by foundational physical relationships.

Large Language Models

Two OpenAI GPT models are employed in this work: GPT-4 and GPT-5. GPT-4, a large multimodal model, demonstrated significant improvements over its predecessors in reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and scientific knowledge retrieval [20]. For GPT-4, the temperature parameter is set to 0.1 to promote reproducible reasoning while allowing limited variability.
